extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; critics and writers interested in criteria for evaluating poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for judging poets and poetic works (especially lyric/short pieces and collected volumes), focusing on moral substance, relation to life, style vs. philosophy, arrangement, and the overall body of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: The noble and profound application of ideas to life
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet receives his distinctive character of superiority from his application ... to his subject ... of the ideas 'On man, on nature, and on human life.' (quoted: 'the noble and profound application of ideas to life')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poet applies ideas about human life, nature, and mankind to poetic subject-matter in a powerful and beautiful way. Examples cited: Wordsworth's superiority arises from his powerful use of such ideas; Voltaire's praise of English poets treating moral ideas with energy and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as criticism of life ('deals with life')
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is at bottom a criticism of life; the greatness of a poet lies in his powerful and beautiful application of ideas to life — to the question: How to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems by how they interrogate, illuminate, or give shape to questions of living and human conduct rather than by technical cleverness alone. A poetry indifferent to such engagement risks being 'a poetry of indifference towards life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of moral ideas (broadly defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral ideas — broadly taken as whatever bears upon 'how to live' — should be treated energetically and deeply in poetry; this is a distinguishing feature of great English poetry (Voltaire's point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work addresses moral questions in a way that is integrated with poetic beauty rather than narrow, pedantic, or merely doctrinal didacticism. Moral content should enrich poetic truth, not reduce it to sermonising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth over philosophical abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages of abstract philosophy or 'a tissue of elevated but abstract verbiage' lack the characters of poetic truth and can be alien to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ideas expressed as genuine poetic insight (poetic truth) and those presented as abstract philosophical doctrine. Long, systematic philosophising within a poem (e.g., in the Excursion) is a sign that the poem may fail as poetry even if the doctrine is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid resting in style or argument (form is an inn, not the destination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style, the play of the senses, literary form and argumentative ingenuity are like inns on the road — attractive but only places of passage; the poet must not make them the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work treats form and stylistic cleverness as means to convey life/ideas rather than as ends in themselves. Criticism should penalize works that stay in 'the inn' of style without pursuing the larger moral or human aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curation: clear away inferior work that obscures the best
rubrics_metrics.description: The bulk of inferior work in a poet's collected volumes can obscure and 'clog' the perception of the poet's best work; 'Wordsworth needs to be relieved of a great deal of the poetical baggage which now encumbers him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a poet, consider both individual pieces and the effect of collection/selection. Recommend editorial curation to present the best pieces together so their cumulative effect is sustained and visible to readers and posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and sustaining impression in collections
rubrics_metrics.description: In a collection of short pieces the impression made by one piece requires to be continued and sustained by the piece following; mixing first-rate pieces with very inferior ones dulls and spoils the overall effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sequencing and relative quality within volumes—look for collections that maintain rather than interrupt the mood or effect created by strong pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate classification and arrangement of poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordsworth's private scheme (poems of fancy, imagination, sentiment, etc.) is 'ingenious but far-fetched' and unsatisfactory; better to adhere to natural classical categories (epic, dramatic, lyric, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poet's organization clarifies relationships among works and aids reception. Prefer natural, broadly recognized categories that reflect dominant strain or form in each poem rather than abstruse mental-physiological taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of subject-matter — dealing with 'life as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's greatness may rest on the extent to which he 'deals with more of life' and treats life as a whole, not merely isolated moods or gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the breadth of a poet's engagement: does the work address large human concerns and a wide range of life, or is it narrowly focused on limited emotional or technical effects? Wordsworth's superiority is argued to come from dealing with life broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow didacticism; didactic poetry counts as a lower kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Some kinds of poetry are 'lower' than others: the ballad kind is lower; the didactic kind still more so — didactic poetry often counts more for biographical than poetical interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in valuing poetry that is primarily instructive or biographically interesting; assess its poetical merits separately and avoid granting undue credit for didactic intent alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of quality in a poet's prime period
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's really first-rate work may be concentrated in a particular creative period (Wordsworth's 'golden prime' 1798–1808); much other work may be inferior before and after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an author's stature, identify his peak oeuvre and weigh that core body of work heavily, while noting how later/earlier inferior pieces affect overall reputation and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form should fit subject (use prose when subject is familiar)
rubrics_metrics.description: With Shakespeare, 'prose comes in whenever the subject, being more familiar, is unsuited to the majestic English iambic.' Form should follow subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen form and rhythm suit the subject and tone. Penalize mismatches where elevated forms are applied to familiar subjects or vice versa, producing incongruity.
